lesson.title: Reading the Unconscious: Inkblots, Stories, and Their Limits
lesson.summary: Projective tests present people with ambiguous, unstructured stimuli on the theory that they will unconsciously project their own hidden thoughts and feelings onto the material, though the approach has faced substantial scientific criticism.
lesson.body:
Projective tests take the concept of projection, covered earlier in this unit, and turn it into an assessment method. The underlying assumption is that when people are shown something ambiguous and asked to make sense of it, what they see and say will reveal unconscious thoughts, conflicts, and motives that they would not, or could not, report if you simply asked them directly on a questionnaire.

The best known example is the Rorschach Inkblot Test, developed by the Swiss psychiatrist Hermann Rorschach and published in 1921. It consists of a series of symmetrical inkblots, and the person being tested is asked what they see in each one. A different well known example is the Thematic Apperception Test, or TAT, developed by Henry Murray and Christiana Morgan at Harvard in the 1930s. Instead of inkblots, the TAT uses ambiguous drawn scenes of people in unclear situations, and the person is asked to tell a story about what is happening in the picture, what led up to it, and how it will turn out. In both cases the stimulus itself is deliberately vague, on the theory that the structure a person imposes on that ambiguity comes from within them.

It is useful to compare projective tests directly with standardized personality testing. A standardized inventory presents fixed questions with fixed answer choices, true or false, or a numbered agreement scale, and is scored the same mechanical way for every test taker, which is part of what makes it standardized. Projective tests work in almost the opposite way: the response is open ended, and turning that response into a score or interpretation requires a trained clinician's judgment.

That reliance on clinical judgment is exactly where projective tests have drawn their most serious criticism. Different examiners scoring the same response have sometimes reached noticeably different conclusions about what it means, which is a reliability problem, and there has been extensive debate over whether scores from these tests actually predict the personality traits, disorders, or behaviors they claim to measure, which is a validity problem. Attempts to fix this, such as John Exner's Comprehensive System for scoring the Rorschach, tried to make the process more standardized and evidence based, and did improve matters somewhat, but reviews of the research have continued to find real limits on how reliable and valid these tests are, especially compared to well validated standardized inventories. Projective tests are still used by some clinicians today, often as one part of a larger assessment battery rather than a stand alone diagnostic tool, but they occupy a much more contested place in the field than standardized testing does, and it is worth understanding them as historically influential and clinically persistent rather than as scientifically settled.
